sample_tweets.text: 🔎 21 EMAIL ADDRESS TOOLS FOR OSINT INVESTIGATIONS  An email address can be one of the strongest pivot points in an investigation.  From a single address, investigators may be able to uncover linked accounts, breach exposure, domain relationships, professional identities, reputation signals, and other infrastructure clues.  Useful tools include:  * GHunt — Google-account OSINT * Castrick — reverse email lookup * EmailRep — email reputation * BreachDirectory — public breach search * LeakCheck — leak exposure search * Hunter.io — professional email finder * SimpleLogin — email alias privacy * Epieos — email reverse lookup * Holehe — linked-account discovery * Have I Been Pwned — breach lookup * Whoxy — WHOIS / reverse WHOIS * theHarvester — email & domain discovery * That’s Them — people-search pivot * Proton Mail — secure email service * OSINT Industries — real-time email lookup * Mailcat — email by username * DeHashed — credential & breach search * XposedOrNot — exposure check * SignalHire — business email finder * Skymem — company email finder * Intelligence X — email data search  The important part is not using all 21 tools.  It is knowing which pivot to use next.  A practical workflow may look like:  * Start with reputation and breach exposure * Look for linked accounts and usernames * Pivot into domains, WHOIS, and infrastructure * Enrich professional or organizational context * Correlate results across independent sources * Preserve URLs, timestamps, and evidence * Separate confirmed facts from assumptions  Analyst Note:  No single OSINT platform should be treated as definitive.  The strongest findings come from correlation: multiple independent sources pointing to the same identity, relationship, or infrastructure.  Use these tools legally, ethically, and with appropriate authorization.  #DDW #OSINT #CyberSecurity #ThreatIntelligence #DigitalInvestigation #EmailOSINT #OpenSourceIntelligence

🇹🇼🚨 1TB+ ASUS DATABASE ALLEGEDLY OFFERED FOR SALE  A threat actor has posted a new dark web listing claiming to possess a 1,023.67 GB database belonging to ASUS.  The seller claims the dataset is being privately offered for sale and published several purported samples as proof of possession.  At this stage, the listing does not provide enough information to determine:  * What systems or ASUS business units are allegedly affected * What categories of information are contained in the ~1TB dataset * When the alleged compromise occurred * Whether the data is newly obtained or previously exposed material * How the actor allegedly obtained access  ⚠️ Analyst Note:  The claimed volume is substantial, but dataset size alone does not establish the authenticity or impact of a breach.  The actor provides very limited technical information and appears to have a newly established forum presence. The purported proof should therefore be treated cautiously until the samples can be independently connected to ASUS infrastructure or ASUS confirms an incident.  For now, this should be considered an unverified threat-actor claim.  #DDW #DarkWeb #ASUS #DataBreach

🇺🇸🇨🇦🚨 NEXUS-LINKED IDENTITY DATASET RESURFACES — ACTOR CLAIMS 195 MILLION RECORDS  A new dark web listing claims to offer approximately 195 million U.S. and Canadian identity records, potentially representing a major development in the Nexus driver’s-license investigation.  The seller, operating as “shinymontanna,” claims they have possessed the data for years and references the now-offline Nexus service directly.  Most notably, the listing contains the same 153,347,439 driver's-license record count previously associated with Nexus.  The seller claims the collection includes:  * 153,347,439 driver's-license records * 10,335,678 identification-card records * 5,092,107 uncategorized records * 1,924,144 travel documents * 1,379,886 international DL/ID records * 579,201 medical-card records * 429,314 Common Access Card records * 91,873 residence-card records * 77,155 employment-authorization records  The actor also claims the dataset affects customers associated with numerous major organizations across retail, transportation, financial services, gaming and other industries.  ⚠️ Analyst Note:  This does NOT necessarily mean Nexus itself has returned.  The identical 153,347,439 driver's-license count strongly suggests a relationship with the dataset previously offered through Nexus. Possible explanations include redistribution of the Nexus collection, multiple actors possessing copies of the same data, or access to a common upstream source.  The FBI is already investigating the underlying Nexus incident.  The new seller’s claim of approximately 195 million records, the affected-company list and their assertion that they possessed the dataset before Nexus should currently be treated as unverified threat-actor claims.  This may indicate the Nexus dataset is beginning to proliferate beyond its original marketplace,  potentially making containment substantially more difficult.  #DDW #DarkWeb #DataBreach #ThreatIntelligence

🇷🇺 RUSSIAN COLLEGE DATA ALLEGEDLY LEAKED  A threat actor has published data allegedly obtained from the Chelyabinsk branch of the Ural College of Economics (УРСЭИ), including information mapping the institution’s academic and administrative structure.  According to the listing, the exposed information includes:  * 23 academic staff records with academic credentials * 105 student groups across multiple courses and education formats * 65 teachers mapped to the groups they teach * 168 subjects and 33 classrooms * 31 administrative staff records, including names, departments, positions and office information * Institutional contact emails and internal phone information * Organizational and teaching-load information  The actor also published sample data and provided what they claim is the complete dataset.  ⚠️ Analyst Note:  This appears more focused on institutional and personnel intelligence than a large-scale student PII breach. Detailed staff identities, roles, contact information and organizational relationships could nevertheless support targeted phishing, impersonation and reconnaissance against the institution.  The authenticity and completeness of the dataset have not been independently verified.  #DDW #DataBreach #Russia #DarkWeb

🚨 PENTAGON REPORTEDLY POLYGRAPHED ~50 PERSONNEL IN CLASSIFIED LEAK INVESTIGATION  The Pentagon reportedly subjected roughly 50 military officers and civilian employees assigned to the Joint Staff to polygraph examinations as part of an investigation into leaks of classified information.  According to The New York Times, the examinations took place in August and focused on determining whether personnel had disclosed classified information to journalists.  The investigation reportedly included questions related to leaked information about U.S. munitions inventories and readiness.  * Roughly 50 Joint Staff personnel reportedly underwent polygraphs * The examinations were part of an internal classified-information leak investigation * Personnel were reportedly questioned about contacts with journalists and unauthorized disclosures * The Pentagon has not publicly identified a suspected leaker * DoD has declined to discuss the specifics of internal personnel or investigative matters  Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell told reporters that the department takes leaks of classified national-security information extremely seriously and investigates them accordingly.  ⚠️ Analyst Note:  Regardless of the politics surrounding individual leaks, this is fundamentally an insider-threat and counterintelligence issue.  Highly classified environments operate on more than technical access controls.  When sensitive information leaves those environments, investigators may have to reconstruct:  Who had access → Who knew the information → Who communicated externally → When the disclosure occurred.  The reported scale of the polygraph effort illustrates how difficult attribution can become when a large number of cleared personnel legitimately have access to the same intelligence.  Important: The specific details of the polygraph operation come from The New York Times' reporting based on officials familiar with the investigation. ♟️🤖 ELON MUSK VS. CHESS.COM: WILL AI EVENTUALLY "SOLVE" CHESS?  Elon Musk and Chess.com just got into a surprisingly technical argument over the future of chess and artificial superintelligence.  It started when Musk argued:  "The actual number of moves that are not utterly stupid in chess is tiny and chess will be fully solved one day."  Chess.com's response?  "skill issue"  Musk doubled down:  "Chess is hard for humans, but not for computers. One day, it will be fully solved like checkers."  Chess.com then brought out the mathematics.  The platform argued that there are roughly 40 orders of magnitude more possible chess games than atoms in the observable universe, suggesting that exhaustively mapping every possible game is effectively impossible.  Musk responded that Chess.com was comparing the wrong thing.  He argued that the number of LEGAL CHESS POSITIONS is roughly 40 orders of magnitude smaller than the estimated number of atoms in the universe.  Then came the AI argument:  Musk predicts that future Artificial Superintelligence won't need to brute-force every possible game.  Instead, he believes ASI will discover ways to solve and compress the chess problem that are "far beyond what we could possibly comprehend."  And then the exchange became personal.  Musk joked:  "Here I am arguing with some random intern at a chess website 🤦‍♂️"  Chess.com replied:  "I'm a full-time employee."  Musk: 😮‍💨  ⚠️ WHO IS ACTUALLY RIGHT?  Interestingly, the numerical disagreement isn't as straightforward as it looks.  Chess.com was talking about possible GAMES, sequences of moves.  Musk was talking about legal POSITIONS, possible board states.  Those are fundamentally different quantities.  But neither number proves Musk's bigger prediction.  Chess engines are already vastly stronger than humans, and endgames with seven or fewer pieces have been exhaustively solved using tablebases.  Chess as a whole, however, has NOT been solved.  Whether future AI, or hypothetical ASI, can eventually strongly solve chess without exhaustively enumerating its enormous search space remains an open question.  This funny exchange actually touches on a serious AI question:  Does sufficiently advanced intelligence overcome computational complexity through better reasoning and abstraction?  Today's chess engines don't examine every possible chess game.  They aggressively reduce the search space using evaluation, pruning and learned representations.  Future AI could potentially discover dramatically better abstractions.  Musk is essentially betting that intelligence will eventually overcome a search problem that currently looks computationally astronomical.  Chess.com's answer is simpler:  Good luck. ♟️  Source: Elon Musk / Chess.com — X, September 3–4, 2026  #AI #Chess #ElonMusk #ASI

A shorter release cycle can reduce the time between upstream Firefox security changes and their arrival in the Tor/Tails ecosystem.  For journalists, researchers, activists, threat-intelligence analysts and others relying on these platforms:  Anonymity does not replace endpoint security.  Keeping Tor Browser and Tails current remains part of the security model. This video may be fun, but it's wrong.  I'm a pro-data-center libertarian. I love @reason. The video is still problematic.  There are a variety of complaints about water use. The biggest is about MUNICIPAL water use, the fact that they sometimes tap into city treated water supplies for EVAPORATIVE COOLING. The worry is it raises how much local residents pay for water.  Trying to fight this with AGRICULTURAL water use, which is not treated water, or shifting to CLOSED LOOP systems, is therefore effectively lying. That's why golf courses and lawns are a better comparison, as they, too, draw from municipal treated water.  But in any case, what a single data center does does not reflect what they all do. In general, the new hyperscalar data-centers aren't pulling from municipal supplies, and if they do, the data-center companies are paying to upgrade the systems so that they don't impact what consumers pay for water, so it's a non-issue.  There are other claims they make about water. For example, they sometimes count the water passing through a dam to generate electricity as part of a data-center's water use. This is a lie so egregious on their part that talking about almonds still can't combat it.  The video then tries to be reasonable about taxes, admitting maybe there's an issue here with the sales tax breaks they get. Nope, there isn't. @reason has just fallen victim to misinformation.  Data-centers are ultimately tax WINDFALLS for local communities. Local communities give them tax breaks because in the long run, they produce huge amounts of money.  This @reason video describes a "hole" in their budgets. That's not true. Data-centers consume almost no local resources (that they don't otherwise pay for themselves). Spending doesn't increase because there's a local data-center. Taxes produced by whatever used to be there are insignificant.  When they build a $5 billion data-center full of expensive GPUs, that creates an insane amount of sales/use taxes and then yearly property-taxes.  Therefore, local governments give tax breaks to lure data-centers because, in the long run, it means a huge stream of free money.  The video mentions Loudon County which has 13% of data centers in the US. They generate so much property tax revenue that the count has lowered property taxes for all the other residents. Another good example is Richland Parish in Lousiana, which technically abates property taxes as well as sales/use taxes -- but gets PILOT payments instead -- "payments in leiu of taxes", which they are spending on bonuses for teachers and infrastructure improvements for local residenets.  Critics like to say that these tax breaks for jobs is a bad idea because they don't generate jobs. This is nonsense, because the reason for tax breaks is to generate more money. Data-centers are a net contribution to local budgets, windfalls. Now, local members of government who negotiate these deals also brag about how they are creating jobs, but as we libertarians know, any such claims are suspect, whether we are talking data-centers, sportsball stadiums, or whatever. Politicians like to pretend they are running the economy when it's the free market that does so. With that said, these data-centers create more permanent jobs than they think. Data-centers exploiting provisions designed to lure factories are nonetheless generating enough jobs to meet those criteria.  The point is that while this @reason video is fun, and it's not terribly accurate. I would never point people to it in order to refute their arguments.

- **Chrome 업데이트**: CVE-2026-85046 악용 사례가 확인되었으므로 즉시 최신 버전으로 업데이트 수행.

- **웹사이트 무결성 검사**: 워드프레스 및 프레스타숍 기반 사이트 관리자는 블록체인 기반 ClickFix 악성 스크립트 삽입 여부 점검.
